\section[lo scontro]{lo scontro — the crash, the collision; the clash}

\label{lesson:IT-C299-scontro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the attack, then the Italian for to threaten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lo scontro}
\textbf{lo scontro} — \textquotedblleft{}the crash, the collision; the clash\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sull'autostrada c'è stato uno scontro tra due camion.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a crash between two lorries on the motorway.}
\end{quote}

Also a clash of ideas or of teams.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{scontro} is built on \emph{scontrare}, a form of \emph{incontrare} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{in contrā} \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lo scontro}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lo scontro}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{lo scontro}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the attack, then the Italian for to threaten, then say \emph{lo scontro} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does lo scontro mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The crash, the collision; the clash\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[scontrarsi]{scontrarsi — to collide}

\label{lesson:IT-C299-scontrarsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to threaten, then the Italian for the crash.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scontrarsi}
\textbf{scontrarsi} — \textquotedblleft{}to collide\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Due auto si sono scontrate all'incrocio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Two cars collided at the crossroads.}
\end{quote}

With \emph{essere}: \emph{si sono scontrate}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{scontrarsi} is the verb behind \emph{scontro}, built on \emph{incontrare}, from Latin \emph{in contrā} \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to threaten, then the Italian for the crash, then say \emph{scontrarsi} again

\section[schiantarsi]{schiantarsi — to crash into something}

\label{lesson:IT-C299-schiantarsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the crash, then the Italian for to collide.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: schiantarsi}
\textbf{schiantarsi} — \textquotedblleft{}to crash into something\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La moto si è schiantata contro un muro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The motorbike crashed into a wall.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Schiantarsi contro} qualcosa.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{schiantarsi} is built on \emph{schiantare} \textquotedblleft{}to split, to break with a crack\textquotedblright{}; its origin is not settled (EtymDB has no entry).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[ammaccare]{ammaccare — to dent, to bruise}

\label{lesson:IT-C299-ammaccare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to collide, then the Italian for to crash into something.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ammaccare}
\textbf{ammaccare} — \textquotedblleft{}to dent, to bruise\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ho ammaccato la macchina nel parcheggio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I dented the car in the car park.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ammaccato} — dented; for fruit, bruised.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ammaccare} is traced in EtymDB to Latin \emph{maccāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bruise, to crush\textquotedblright{}, a word whose own origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[danneggiare]{danneggiare — to damage}

\label{lesson:IT-C299-danneggiare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to crash into something, then the Italian for to dent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: danneggiare}
\textbf{danneggiare} — \textquotedblleft{}to damage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il vento ha danneggiato il tetto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The wind damaged the roof.}
\end{quote}

Present \emph{danneggio}, \emph{danneggi}, \emph{danneggia}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{danneggiare} is built on \emph{danno} \textquotedblleft{}damage\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{damnum} \textquotedblleft{}loss, harm\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
